examShortTricks: Trick 1: Central claim: tradition survives only when elders are listened to — LaPena blames the young's inattention, not modernity itself; quote the blame line.
Trick 2: The essay's structure is argument by examples (storytelling, art, nature) — answer 'how does the writer support his view?' by listing two examples.
Trick 3: Apply to Nepal: oral traditions, festivals and crafts face the same neglect — one Nepali parallel lifts the answer.
practiceQuestions: Q. According to LaPena, why are traditions being lost? (2 marks) — the young do not listen to elders; modern distractions replace storytelling.
Q. How can young people keep traditions alive? (2 marks) — listen to and record elders' stories; practise and pass on customs.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three stories = three lessons: connecting dots (trust that experiences connect), love and loss (do what you love), death (live each day as your last) — structure every answer around the three.
Trick 2: 'Stay hungry, stay foolish' — the closing motto; explain what each half means (never complacent; take risks).
Trick 3: The 'dots' metaphor: you can only connect them looking BACKWARDS, so trust in the future — the most-quoted line; use it in theme answers.
practiceQuestions: Q. What are the three stories Jobs tells? (3 marks) — connecting the dots; love and loss; death.
Q. What does 'stay hungry, stay foolish' mean? (2 marks) — keep ambition and curiosity alive; dare to take risks.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Haldane lists needs in tiers: work worth doing, freedom, health, companionship — answer 'what does he require?' by the list, not by summary.
Trick 2: The scientist's angle: he demands opportunity for RESEARCH and rational discussion — distinguish his intellectual needs from material ones.
Trick 3: Compare-and-contrast question: Haldane's wants vs an ordinary citizen's — both need freedom and work, but he adds science; state the overlap and difference.
practiceQuestions: Q. What does Haldane require from life? (3 marks) — meaningful work, freedom, health, friendship and scope for science.
Q. Which of Haldane's requirements do you share? Give reasons. (2 marks) — pick one (e.g. meaningful work) and justify personally.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The essay defines poverty through lived detail, not statistics — soap, hot water, rest, dignity; collect three concrete details for any theme answer.
Trick 2: The tone is angry and defiant — she rejects romantic and pitying definitions; tone questions need her own words as evidence.
Trick 3: Key insight: poverty is exhaustion and the loss of future options, not merely lack of money — state this redefinition.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does Parker define poverty? (2 marks) — not just lack of money but exhaustion, bad housing and lost hope/dignity.
Q. What is the tone of the essay? (1 mark) — bitter, defiant, personal.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Thesis: humanity survives because research keeps solving new threats — science as insurance; state the thesis in one line.
Trick 2: The seismologist's examples: earthquake prediction, medicine, energy — pick two of his examples to show 'research = survival'.
Trick 3: Funding argument: basic research looks useless today but pays off tomorrow — the delayed-return logic is the essay's hardest point; explain it with one example.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does the writer call research a token of survival? (2 marks) — every human crisis has been answered by scientific research; future threats need it too.
Q. Why should society fund 'useless' basic research? (2 marks) — today's curiosity becomes tomorrow's cure; give one example (e.g. earthquake studies).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The title's irony: men dismiss 'trifles' (kitchen things) that actually solve the crime — the women find the evidence the men overlook; this reversal is the core answer.
Trick 2: Evidence of motive: the broken birdcage and the dead canary — Minnie's strangled bird mirrors her strangled spirit; connect symbol to motive.
Trick 3: Gender theme: the men's condescension ('women worry over trifles') is exactly why they fail — quote one condescending line and pair it with the women's discovery.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is the play titled 'Trifles'? (2 marks) — the 'trivial' domestic details the men ignore contain the motive the women uncover.
Q. What does the dead canary symbolise? (2 marks) — Minnie Foster's silenced joy; her husband killed it as he killed her spirit.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The play's charm is RECOGNITION: two elderly ex-sweeteners meet as strangers feeding birds and gradually recognise each other — the gradual reveal structure is the answer.
Trick 2: Vanity and age: each pretends to be younger and blames the other for not recognising them — the comic irony of mutual self-deception.
Trick 3: The crumbs and the bench: small props carry nostalgia — link one prop to the theme of lost love and time.
practiceQuestions: Q. How do Dona Laura and Don Gonzalo conceal their identities at first? (2 marks) — each invents a younger self and a fictional past, afraid of ridicule.
Q. What is the theme of the play? (2 marks) — ageing, vanity and the sweet persistence of first love.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Satire target: the education system that certifies without wisdom — Wasserkopf's absurd demand for a refund exposes what schooling failed to teach.
Trick 2: The teachers' counter-trick: they declare him a GENIUS, using his own logic against him — the reversal is the play's climax; explain the logic trap.
Trick 3: The mathematics master's final move (any answer can be 'wrong' or 'right') shows education's real lesson: thinking, not facts — quote the last exchange.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does Wasserkopf demand a refund? (2 marks) — he claims eighteen years of schooling taught him nothing useful; he wants his fees back with interest.
Q. How do the teachers defeat him? (2 marks) — by proving every answer he gives is correct (each wrong answer 'proves' his genius), so no refund is due.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Match structure to type — argumentative: claim → reasons → counter → rebuttal; descriptive: sensory detail; narrative: chronology + climax; expository: explain with facts — name the type before writing.
Trick 2: The 5-paragraph safety net: introduction with thesis, three body paragraphs each with ONE point, conclusion that restates — it fits all four types.
Trick 3: Marks live in the THESIS sentence: state your position in the last line of the introduction; a vague thesis caps the band.
Trick 4: Cohesion devices: firstly, moreover, however, in conclusion — use 4–5 linking words; examiners tick them.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the introduction of an argumentative essay on social media with a clear thesis. (3 marks) — hook, context, thesis stating your position.
Q. How does a narrative essay differ from an expository one? (1 mark) — narrative tells a story in time order; expository explains ideas with facts.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Formats earn marks — letter to the editor: sender's address, date, editor's address, salutation 'Sir/Madam', subject line, body (problem→effects→request), 'Yours faithfully'; job application adds CV reference line.
Trick 2: Complaint letters: state the FACT (what, when, where), the LOSS, and the REMEDY you want — three paragraphs, no emotion without evidence.
Trick 3: Subject line and 'Yours faithfully/truly' choice (faithfully when 'Dear Sir') — the two format details most students lose.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a letter to the editor about road accidents in your town. (4 marks) — format + problem with one example + two causes + two suggestions.
Q. What goes in the subject line of a complaint letter? (1 mark) — a concise statement of the complaint, e.g. 'Complaint about frequent power cuts'.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Report skeleton: title, byline, intro (what/when/where), body (details in past tense, third person), conclusion (outcome/recommendation) — the five blocks are the marks.
Trick 2: Reports are OBJECTIVE: no 'I think', no exaggeration; add one quotation or number for credibility.
Trick 3: Summary method: read twice → one line per paragraph → join with connectors → compress to 1/3 length in your own words; never copy sentences.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a report on a school science exhibition in about 120 words. (4 marks) — title, byline, 5W intro, two body details, closing outcome.
Q. How long should a summary be? (1 mark) — about one-third of the original, in your own words.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Story skeleton: setting → conflict → rising action → climax → resolution; plan the CLIMAX first, then work backwards — plots fail without a designed turning point.
Trick 2: Show, don't tell: replace 'he was scared' with 'his hands shook as he reached the door' — one shown detail per paragraph lifts the band.
Trick 3: Dialogue rule: every line of dialogue must reveal character or advance plot; two lines are better than five flat ones.
Trick 4: Title and moral: end with a line that echoes the title — circular closure earns the structure mark.
practiceQuestions: Q. Develop a story beginning: 'It was raining heavily that night...' (5 marks) — set scene, introduce conflict, climax, resolution with a title.
Q. What makes a story's climax effective? (1 mark) — it resolves the central conflict at maximum tension.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Speech frame: greeting → attention hook (question/quote/statistic) → three points with signposting ('firstly... secondly...') → memorable close (call to action).
Trick 2: Write for the EAR: short sentences, direct address ('my friends'), rhetorical questions — spoken rhythm is the style mark.
Trick 3: Time yourself: a 3-minute speech ≈ 350–400 words — over-length speeches lose the discipline mark.
practiceQuestions: Q. Prepare a 2-minute speech on the importance of voting. (4 marks) — greeting, hook, two arguments, call to action.
Q. How should a speech begin? (1 mark) — with a greeting and an attention-grabbing hook.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Review anatomy: title/creator → one-line premise (no spoilers) → two strengths → one weakness → verdict with a rating — the five-part frame.
Trick 2: Judge against PURPOSE, not taste: a thriller must thrill, a documentary must inform — state the criterion before judging.
Trick 3: Use the vocabulary bank: plot, pacing, characterisation, cinematography, narrative arc — technical terms lift the band instantly.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a short review of a film you have recently watched. (4 marks) — premise, one strength with example, one weakness, verdict.
Q. What must a review avoid? (1 mark) — major spoilers and purely personal bias without criteria.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Note-making format: title → indented points → sub-points (a, b) → abbreviations with a key; the visual format itself carries marks.
Trick 2: Keep only ONE idea per point; drop examples, repetitions and statistics — selection is the tested skill.
Trick 3: Summary vs notes: summary is connected prose in your own words; notes are fragments — do not mix the two forms.
practiceQuestions: Q. Make notes on a passage with a title and three main points. (3 marks) — heading, indented points with sub-points, key to abbreviations.
Q. What should be excluded from a summary? (1 mark) — examples, repetition and minor details.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Read the QUESTIONS first, then the passage — you read once with a target instead of twice blindly.
Trick 2: Answer in your OWN words unless quoting is asked; lift-and-drop answers lose the paraphrase mark.
Trick 3: Vocabulary-in-context: replace the word with each option and reread the sentence — grammar fit eliminates two options immediately.
Trick 4: Inference questions: the answer is NOT written; combine two clues and start 'This suggests that...'
practiceQuestions: Q. How should you answer an inference question? (1 mark) — combine clues from the text and state what they imply, in your own words.
Q. Why read the questions before the passage? (1 mark) — to read purposefully and locate answers faster.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Clause ID: independent = complete thought; dependent = starts with subordinator (because, although, when); relative = who/which/that + verb — classify before combining.
Trick 2: Comma rules that pay: after introductory phrases, around non-essential clauses, before coordinating conjunctions joining two full clauses; semicolon joins two related full sentences.
Trick 3: Sentence variety for writing marks: mix a simple, a compound and a complex sentence in every paragraph — uniform simple sentences cap the style band.
Trick 4: Fragment test: read the sentence aloud alone — if it leaves a question hanging ('because he was late'), it is a fragment.
practiceQuestions: Q. Identify the clause type: 'Although it rained, we played.' (1 mark) — dependent adverbial clause + independent clause (complex sentence).
Q. Fix the fragment: 'Because he was tired.' (1 mark) — attach an independent clause: 'Because he was tired, he slept early.'

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The unit's skill set: question assumptions, check evidence, spot bias, consider alternatives — answer 'what is critical thinking?' with these four verbs.
Trick 2: Evaluate any text with three questions: Who wrote it and why? What evidence supports it? What is left out? — the omission question is the most revealing.
Trick 3: In argumentative answers, steel-man the opposition (state its best form) before refuting — it demonstrates critical distance.
practiceQuestions: Q. What does it mean to think critically? (2 marks) — questioning assumptions and evaluating evidence before accepting a claim.
Q. Why check what a text leaves out? (1 mark) — omissions can bias the argument as much as false claims.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Analysis ladder: device → effect → theme — never stop at naming a device; the marks are in what it ACHIEVES and what it MEANS.
Trick 2: Every interpretation must be text-anchored: claim + quotation + explanation; a claim without quotation sits in the lower band.
Trick 3: Title, opening line and ending carry authorial intent — analyse all three when asked about the writer's purpose.
practiceQuestions: Q. How do you analyse a literary device? (2 marks) — name it, quote it, explain its effect on meaning or mood.
Q. Why does the title matter in interpretation? (1 mark) — it often condenses the theme or irony the work develops.
